objection: Does ‘firstborn of creation’ mean Jesus was created?
answer:
This is a fair pressure-point, and it deserves a direct answer rather than a dodge.

First, the linguistic point stands independent of the polemical context: πρωτότοκος was already a title of rank in Jewish usage before Colossians was written — Psalm 89:27 calls David God's "firstborn" though he was neither God's first nor only son in any literal sense. Paul didn't need Gnostic pressure to reach for that word; it was standard idiom for supremacy and inheritance-status. So the "borrowed because it needed defending" theory has the explanation backwards — the word already carried the rank sense Paul needed, which is presumably why he chose it.

Second, your own argument actually proves the orthodox reading rather than undermining it. You note that if Jesus were part of the created order, he'd be subject to the very powers he rules over in 1:16 — that's exactly the point Colossians 1:15–20 is making about him: he is placed on the Creator side of a Creator-creature distinction, not folded into "all things." Paul doesn't reach for ambiguous language and hope preeminence sticks; he immediately disambiguates in the next breath — "for by him were all things created" — precisely so no reader could take prototokos temporally. If he'd meant "first creature," verse 16 makes him the Creator of himself, which is incoherent.

Third, notice this isn't an isolated move under polemical duress. The same conceptual pattern — Son as agent of all creation, therefore not himself created — appears in John 1:3 and Hebrews 1, texts not addressed to Colossae's crisis at all. That cross-textual consistency argues against "ad hoc adaptation" and for settled apostolic conviction that simply gets deployed with sharpened precision when a rival cosmology forces the issue. Controversy can occasion clearer statement of a belief without having generated the belief itself — that's consistent with, not contrary to, the pre-existence already being apostolic bedrock.
